can_do_statement: Can use 'may have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When you guess about what happened before now, use 'may have' plus the past participle.

positives: He may have forgiven me for that accident.
As you may have noticed, there has been a delay.
negatives: He may have a new car.
May we have some water?

can_do_statement: Can use 'may I' to make a polite request for permission.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To ask for permission in a formal or polite way, start with 'May I'.

positives: Sir, may I come in?
May I ask you if your special offer will be still available?
negatives: He may go to the store.
The month of May is warm.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may well' to give emphasis to something unexpected.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When something is very likely, you can say it 'may well' happen.

positives: I think they may well come to an agreement.
It may well be that after leaving school they become our employees.
negatives: He may do well on the exam.
The well may dry up.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may' in phrases such as as 'you may know', or 'as you may have' + '-ed' to focus the reader on shared knowledge.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To remind someone of something they probably know, use 'as you may know' or 'as you may have heard'.

positives: As you may know, it takes many hours.
As you may have heard, I am going to change to the engineering department.
negatives: You may leave when you are ready.
He may know the answer to the question.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may … but' to express an unexpected point of view.

ontology.mental_model: Conceding a point before introducing a counter-argument
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To agree with something briefly before adding a surprising twist, use 'may' followed by 'but'.

positives: This may surprise you but I've managed to lose some weight.
You may think that it is quite boring but it is not.
negatives: He may go to the store, but I don't think he will.
May I go? But why?

can_do_statement: Can use 'may as well' to talk about what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative or when it will not spoil the situation if you do that thing. ► might

ontology.mental_model: Accepting the most logical course of action
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When there's no better alternative, you can say you 'may as well' do something.

positives: After all, you may as well know.
I may as well see the other things.
negatives: He may do as well as she did.
She may well win the race.

can_do_statement: Can use 'it may be' + '-ed' that as a hedging device when drawing conclusions and summarising, particularly in academic contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: In academic writing, use 'it may be argued that' to soften your statements.

positives: It may be concluded that their ultimate aim remains unchanged.
It may be argued that a child's academic success is crucial.
negatives: It may be that he is right.
The car may be parked there.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may' in a subordinate clause expressing concession with 'however', 'whatever', 'whoever' … + 'it or this may be or seem'.

ontology.mental_model: Conceding a point regardless of conditions
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To say that something is true no matter what, use 'whatever it may be' or 'however it may seem'.

positives: However small it may be, I love it.
People enjoy what they are doing whatever it may be.
negatives: However, it may be true.
Whatever you do, you may be happy.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To talk about something that is possible, use 'might' with a base verb.

positives: The weather might be hot and sunny.
I think it might be in your bedroom.
negatives: It might not be true.
I shouldn't do this.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might' to make polite suggestions and give advice.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To give gentle advice or suggest an idea politely, tell someone 'you might' do something.

positives: You might need to bring some food and drink.
I think that you might talk with your parents.
negatives: He might talk to his parents.
You might be late.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility with a past reference.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To talk about what was possible in the past, use 'might have' with the past participle.

positives: Many things might have led to these changes.
I thought that a burglar might have broken into our house.
negatives: He might have a lot of money.
She might have to leave early.

ontology.mental_model: Forming the past modal of possibility
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To make 'might' past tense, add 'have' and a past participle.

positives: It might have been our neighbours' cat.
He might have seen us.
negatives: They might have some issues.
I might have to go now.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might' as the past form of 'may' in indirect reports.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When reporting what someone said using 'may', change it to 'might'.

positives: My parents said it might be the last holiday.
Lisa thought it might be a lucky one so she showed it to her Dad.
negatives: It might rain today.
They say it might snow tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might' to talk about weak possibility.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: If something is only a small possibility, use 'might' instead of 'will'.

positives: He might take us.
It might be on the computer table.
negatives: I might not know.
I shouldn't do this.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To say it's possible something won't happen, use 'might not' or 'mightn't'.

positives: It might not be very fashionable.
This mightn't be such a good thing.
negatives: It might be a problem.
She might go to the store.
